content: Drotrecogin-α (Xigris®) is primarily utilized in the treatment of severe sepsis. Tickborne relapsing fever (TBRF) is a bacterial illness caused by specific Borrelia species and transmitted through brief, painless bites from Ornithodoros ticks. The disease is typically characterized by intermittent episodes of fever, fatigue, and muscle aches. In April 2005, the CDC received reports of two cases of severe TBRF associated with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in residents of California and Nevada. Following a report on these cases posted on the CDC's Epidemic Information Exchange (Epi-X), health officials in Washington reported a third severe case linked to ARDS. This report summarizes these three cases and the findings of subsequent epidemiologic investigations, which suggest that ARDS may occur more frequently in TBRF patients than previously recognized. Effective management of TBRF requires prompt diagnosis and careful monitoring during the initial phases of treatment. Case Reports: Nevada On February 17, 2005, a previously healthy 46-year-old woman from Washoe County, Nevada, developed nonspecific leg pain, which progressed to generalized myalgia within 24 hours. She visited a local emergency department (ED), where she was diagnosed with a viral syndrome, treated with intravenous (IV) fluids and pain medication, and discharged. Two days later, she returned to the ED with fever, chills, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, and a syncopal episode. Physical examination was unremarkable except for a fever of 102°F. Pulse oximetry on room air showed an oxygen saturation of 96%. Laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 4 × 10³/µL, hemoglobin of 13 g/dL, platelet count of 66 × 10³/µL, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 153 U/L. A chest radiograph revealed a right middle lobe infiltrate consistent with community-acquired pneumonia. She was treated with gatifloxacin and admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Approximately 10 hours after admission, she was intubated for worsening tachypnea (respiratory rate: 40 breaths per minute). Chest radiographs showed diffuse bilateral infiltrates, and arterial blood gas analysis revealed oxygenation of 53 mmHg on 100% inspired oxygen. Antimicrobial therapy was broadened to include vancomycin and doxycycline. The next day, spirochetes were observed on a manually reviewed blood smear obtained at admission due to thrombocytopenia. The patient remained intubated for 12 days for ARDS and was discharged after 21 days, recovering completely. Borrelia hermsii was identified as the causative organism via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on a whole blood sample and serologic testing of convalescent-phase serum, both performed at the CDC. Although the patient did not recall a tick bite, she reported staying at a resort near South Lake Tahoe, a highly endemic area for TBRF, five days before becoming ill. Case Reports: California On April 12, 2005, a previously healthy 43-year-old woman from El Dorado County, California, developed lethargy and myalgia. She visited a local ED on April 14 with fever, chills, headache, myalgia, and dehydration. She was febrile (101.5°F), tachycardic (138 bpm), mildly tachypneic (16 breaths per minute), and hypotensive (systolic blood pressure: 97 mmHg). Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, and pulse oximetry on room air showed an oxygen saturation of 97%. Laboratory findings included a creatinine level of 1.6 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 93 U/L, and ALT of 88 U/L. She was treated with acetaminophen and discharged with instructions to return for reevaluation the next day. Upon return, she presented with headache, sweating, fatigue, and nausea. Physical examination revealed rhonchi, but a chest radiograph was normal. She was treated with IV fluids and IV ceftriaxone. Within one hour of receiving antibiotics, her pulse increased to 127 bpm, systolic blood pressure dropped to 85 mmHg, and oxygen saturation on room air was 95%. TBRF was diagnosed by observing spirochetes in peripheral blood smears. She was treated with dopamine for hypotension and doxycycline for TBRF and transferred to another medical center. Shortly after arrival, a chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral infiltrates due to worsening respiratory distress. She was intubated for respiratory failure (respiratory rate: 44 breaths per minute; oxygen saturation: 82% on 100% inspired oxygen via non-rebreather mask) attributed to ARDS. Laboratory findings included a hemoglobin level of 9.4 g/dL and a platelet count of 19 × 10³/µL. Platelets and fresh frozen plasma were administered. She remained intubated for 10 days, during which she received four different antimicrobials (vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, metronidazole, and doxycycline) and drotrecogin-α. She was discharged after 19 days of hospitalization and eventually recovered. A blood sample obtained early in her illness and cultured at the CDC yielded Borrelia hermsii. An environmental investigation at her home, located near Lake Tahoe, revealed an engorged soft tick in her bedroom and multiple rodent nests with approximately 30 Ornithodoros hermsi ticks. Case Reports: Washington A 40-year-old woman from King County, Washington, visited an ED on September 21, 2004, with myalgia, arthralgia, nausea, vomiting, and headache. She was treated with IV fluids, promethazine, and hydrocodone but refused hospital admission. After experiencing a syncopal episode at home, she returned to the ED and was noted to be febrile (102°F), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure: 100 mmHg), mildly tachycardic (107 bpm), and hypoxic (oxygen saturation: 92% on 4 L of oxygen). Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable. A chest radiograph revealed bilateral lower lobe infiltrates. Laboratory findings included a white blood cell count of 5 × 10³/µL, hematocrit of 33%, platelet count of 49 × 10³/µL, ALT of 192 U/L, and a D-dimer of 754. She was admitted for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with sepsis and treated empirically with IV cefuroxime and azithromycin. After receiving cefuroxime, she became transiently hypotensive and somnolent. She was intubated and transferred to the ICU with a diagnosis of ARDS and worsening mental status. A peripheral blood smear, examined due to thrombocytopenia, revealed spirochetes diagnostic of TBRF. Her transient hypotension was attributed to a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR). She remained intubated for three days, was discharged home after 10 days, and eventually recovered. The most likely site of exposure was a forest cabin in Chelan County, Washington, where she had stayed approximately 11 days before illness onset. Inspection of the cabin revealed evidence of rodent infestation, but attempts to trap ticks and rodents were unsuccessful. Epidemiologic Investigations To assess the frequency of ARDS among TBRF patients in the South Lake Tahoe area, case-report forms for all TBRF cases reported to Nevada and California health departments from 1995 to 2004 were reviewed. Additional cases were identified through hospital discharge records, interviews with healthcare providers, and postings on Epi-X and the Emerging Infections Network. Including the California and Nevada cases described in this report, 65 TBRF cases were identified among individuals who had lived in or visited the Lake Tahoe area during the usual incubation period of 2–18 days before illness onset. Of these, 46% required hospitalization, and 42% experienced complications such as JHR, hypoxia, elevated liver enzymes, arrhythmia or myocarditis, azotemia, or ARDS.
